# Team Workflow Patterns

This reference covers how teams (not just individuals) coordinate when multiple developers or agents operate in worktrees simultaneously.

For source details, see [citations.md](../citations.md).

## Branch Naming Conventions

No single standard has emerged. At least 6 distinct patterns exist across tools and teams:

| Convention | Example | Source |
|-----------|---------|--------|
| Claude Code default | `worktree-<name>` | [3] |
| Human names | `experimental/alice`, `experimental/bob` | [19] |
| Feature prefix | `feature/descriptive-name` | [9] |
| Subdirectory convention | `.trees/<name>` with any branch name | [16] |
| User-prefixed | `<username>/<feature>` | [7] |
| Tool + hash | `worktree-agent-{hash}` | [discovery] |

The Claude Code default (`worktree-agent-{hash}`) is a known pain point — an open feature request (#27749) exists for custom branch names because opaque hashes make it hard to identify tasks and integrate with naming conventions [discovery].

## PR Volume and Review Bottleneck

AI-assisted worktree workflows dramatically increase PR volume, creating a review bottleneck that multiple sources quantify:

| Metric | Value | Source |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Issues per PR (AI-authored) | 10.83 | [13] |
| Issues per PR (human-only) | 6.45 | [13] |
| Issue ratio (AI/human) | 1.7× | [13] |
| Security issue ratio | 2.74× | [13] |
| Readability issue ratio | 3.0× | [13] |
| Performance regression ratio | ~8.0× | [13] |

**CodeRabbit study parameters:** 470 open-source GitHub PRs (320 AI-authored, 150 human-only), using CodeRabbit's structured issue taxonomy [13].

**Faros AI research** (data from discovery agent, not verified against full article due to TLS failure [24]): Across 10,000+ developers and 1,255 teams, teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs but PR review times increased 91% [24].

## Team Coordination Models

### Hierarchical (Team Lead + Workers)
One agent acts as coordinator, dispatching tasks and managing merges [8][22]:

- Lead: Plans work, delegates to worker agents, determines merge order, resolves conflicts
- Workers: Operate in isolated worktrees, each assigned distinct features
- "The lead breaks down a task, teammates claim subtasks, each works in isolation, and the lead merges the results" [22]

### Self-Organizing (Independent Agents)
Each developer runs their own agents independently. Coordination happens through PR review and CI [7][18]:

- incident.io: 4-5 agents per developer, bash wrapper for management [7]
- Addy Osmani: "spin up a fresh git worktree for a new feature" with commit-early-and-often discipline [18]

### Pipeline (Sequential Roles)
Emerging pattern: Spec Agent → Implementation Agent → Review Agent [discovery]:
- Branch creation is the coordination mechanism
- PR is the review gate
- Each agent role has different tool access and permissions

## Review Strategies for AI-Generated Code

Addy Osmani advocates dual-layer review [18]:
1. **Human review:** Read AI-generated code line-by-line before integration
2. **AI-assisted review:** Spawn secondary AI sessions to critique first-model outputs

Key principle: "AI-written code needs **extra scrutiny**" — "If anything, AI-written code needs extra scrutiny" [18].

**AI PRs show ~1.7× more critical and major findings** than human-written code [13], reinforcing the need for thorough review.

## Commit and Version Control Discipline

Practitioners consistently recommend increased commit frequency when working with AI agents [18][15]:

- Osmani: "I commit early and often, even more than I would in normal hand-coding...like save points in a game" [18]
- matklad: "I just commit whatever and deal with it later" — uses `ggc` utility for atomic "commit all with a trivial message" [15]
- Copilot CLI: Auto-commits at end of each turn [5]

## Context-Switching Cost

Filip Hracek identifies the cognitive load of parallel agent management: "chasing two very fast (and sometimes infuriatingly dumb) LLM agents is incompatible with deep work" [19]. He maintains separate weekly deep work periods without agent coordination.

Intility Engineering acknowledges the pattern "probably works best for less complex tasks and bugfixes" [8] rather than deeply interdependent features.

## Gaps and Limitations

- **Worktree lifecycle management at scale** (10+ developers × 3-5 worktrees each = 30-50 active worktrees) is not addressed.
